difficultyReason: The argument's conclusion depends on a hidden methodological assumption: that the linguistic complexity index reliably tracks cognitive load across typologically distinct languages. The correct weakener attacks this buried premise rather than the surface causal claim, while four distractors each implement a named trap — one strengthener, one too-narrow, one irrelevant, and one that undermines an adjacent premise without touching the conclusion.
stimulus: A team of researchers measured the linguistic complexity of written legal documents in twelve countries, using a standardized index that scores documents on sentence length, syntactic embedding depth, and rare-vocabulary density. Countries whose legal documents scored in the top quartile of the index had court proceedings that lasted, on average, 40 percent longer than those in the bottom quartile. The researchers concluded that reducing the linguistic complexity of legal documents would significantly shorten court proceedings in high-complexity countries.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the researchers' conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The standardized complexity index was developed using documents from languages that share the same grammatical family, and it systematically underscores complexity in languages with different morphological structures, making high-scoring countries disproportionately those with already-efficient court systems.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In several of the twelve countries studied, court proceedings grew longer over the same period in which legal documents became more complex, suggesting that the relationship between the two variables is not merely coincidental.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Legal scholars in countries with the longest court proceedings have independently advocated for plain-language reforms, indicating that practitioners themselves recognize the burden imposed by complex documents.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A pilot program in one high-complexity country reduced the rare-vocabulary density of its civil court filings by 30 percent but had no measurable effect on the duration of criminal proceedings in that country.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Countries with high linguistic complexity scores also tend to have more litigants who represent themselves without counsel, a factor that independently prolongs court proceedings regardless of document complexity.

explanations.correct: The researchers assume the index accurately identifies countries whose legal documents genuinely impose high cognitive or procedural burdens. Choice A reveals that the index is methodologically biased: it underscores complexity in morphologically distinct languages, so countries classified as 'high complexity' are actually those whose languages happen to share the index's grammatical family — and these happen to be countries with efficient courts. This means the correlation between high index scores and longer proceedings may be an artifact of measurement error rather than a genuine relationship, directly undermining the evidential basis for the causal conclusion.
explanations.A: Correct. Attacks the hidden methodological assumption that the index validly measures what it claims to measure across all twelve countries, collapsing the evidentiary foundation for the causal claim.
explanations.B: Opposite-answer trap (strengthener). Noting that complexity and proceeding length grew together over time corroborates the researchers' causal story by reinforcing the temporal correlation; it does not weaken the conclusion.
explanations.C: Shift-in-subject trap. That practitioners advocate for reform is consistent with the researchers' conclusion but does not logically support or weaken it; the source of the advocacy is irrelevant to whether simplification would actually reduce proceeding duration.
explanations.D: Too-narrow trap. The pilot affected only civil filings and measured only criminal proceedings — a scope mismatch that makes the result inconclusive. Even if taken at face value, it attacks only one application of the proposed intervention without showing that the researchers' broader conclusion is wrong.
explanations.E: Confounding-variable trap that sounds like a strong weakener but is not. While self-represented litigants could independently prolong proceedings, this would have to be shown to explain the full 40-percent gap. As stated, it is merely an additional factor that coexists with document complexity; it does not demonstrate that complexity is causally inert, leaving the researchers' conclusion largely intact.
